transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-06-30 16:00 UTC | Duration 47m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood PS), Marta Ruiz (Redwood CSM); Carlos Vega (Ironsail Head of Platform), Lina Ortiz (Cloud Architect), Tom Beck (Security), Evan Shaw (SRE)

Summary: (auto) We talked through Ironsail's need to run Redwood Private in their VPC across eu-west-1 and us-east-1, with strict downstream partner egress IP whitelisting, and an ask for per-environment IP slicing. Discussed options: PrivateLink endpoints, TGW peering, and per-region NAT/EIP allocation.

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intros then we'll jump into the network constraints.
00:12 Carlos Vega: yeah hi, Carlos here, head of platform. Thanks for making time.
00:17 Lina Ortiz: Lina, cloud architect, i'll try to keep notes.
00:22 Alex Chen: great, i'll recap agenda: we want to understand your topology, egress requirements, security, and timelines. Priya will talk about the Private deployment patterns.
00:35 Priya Nambiar: cool, so at a high level Redwood Private supports either managed private endpoints (we call PrivateLink in aws) or peering via transit gateway; both can be used to keep traffic off the public internet.
00:48 Tom Beck: when you say PrivateLink, do you mean AWS PrivateLink service endpoints, or something we host?
00:54 Priya Nambiar: yes aws PrivateLink — basically interface endpoints in your VPC that front the Redwood control plane and inference dataplane. It avoids SNAT for control, but for egress out to third-party APIs you'd still need egress IPs to be predictable.
01:10 Evan Shaw: that's the big one for us — our partners require allowlisting of exact IP ranges, and we run partner systems in multiple regions, so we need a deterministic mapping. We also want dev/test separated so no shared IP space.
01:27 Samir Patel: totally makes sense. There are two common patterns: 1) per-region dedicated NAT/EIP pools (IP slicing) where we pin EIPs to subnets used by Redwood nodes; or 2) route traffic through a central egress VPC with static EIPs via TGW. Each has tradeoffs.
01:46 Lina Ortiz: cost and latency tradeoffs? If we centralize egress the RTT for eu-west-1 calls to partners in eu-west-1 could increase.
01:55 Priya Nambiar: correct — central egress simplifies IP management but adds intra-cloud hop latency. If partner calls are latency sensitive you should keep egress regional.
02:09 Tom Beck: we have another constraint: audit logs must include per-request trace IDs and be pushed to our SIEM, and keys must be via our KMS. How tightly does Redwood integrate with customer KMS?
02:22 Alex Chen: Redwood Private can integrate with customer-managed KMS in the private deployment. We'll include the KMS integration guide and a SOC2 mapping doc.
02:31 Tom Beck: ok cool, want to see that.
02:34 02:34 Priya Nambiar: also note we have a small footprint mode for constrained networks — it reduces outbound connections and supports proactive KV cache warming to avoid cold starts.
02:48 Carlos Vega: can you say more about IP slicing—like how we'd do prod vs stage ranges?
02:54 Samir Patel: yeah typically we allocate distinct EIP pools per environment: e.g., prod: 3 EIPs per AZ, stage: 1 EIP per AZ, etc. We create per-environment subnets and node groups pinned to those subnets so their NAT uses that EIP set. We also provide a mapping doc so you can share allowlist entries with partners.
03:16 Lina Ortiz: do you manage those EIPs or we do?
03:20 Priya Nambiar: in Private deployment we recommend customer-owned EIPs; Redwood's installer can attach those to the instances or to NAT gateways depending on pattern. For Dedicated we can manage on your behalf but for Private your security team usually prefers customer-owned.
03:36 Evan Shaw: got it. Another item: region gating, our legal team only allows data to leave eu regions for EU customers. Can Redwood route model execution to eu-only nodes?
03:48 Priya Nambiar: yes you can pin model routing by region and set routing policies — requests from EU customers can be routed to eu-west-1 nodes. If capacity's constrained we can fallback to a compatible variant but that's controllable via rollout policy.
04:05 Carlos Vega: okay fallback is fine if notified. We need to know latency implications.
04:09 Priya Nambiar: we'll run a sample estimate. We'll need your typical request qps and average seq length.
04:18 Lina Ortiz: approx 5k qps at peak across our two regions, typical seq length 64 tokens.
04:25 Priya Nambiar: perfect — we'll simulate that.
04:28 Tom Beck: about peering, we currently use Transit Gateway for most cross-account traffic, do you have configs for TGW attachments?
04:35 Samir Patel: yes, we have a TGW attachment pattern — basically you attach Redwood subnets to the TGW from our account or from your account depending on your preference; we can also deploy in your account and attach directly. For cross-account TGW we provide an IAM and CF template.
04:52 Carlos Vega: who owns the route tables in that case?
04:55 Samir Patel: you do — we provide recommended route map and a small set of routes for the dataplane subnets, but final route table changes are under your control.
05:05 Lina Ortiz: any constraints re: IP range sizes? we use /16 internal for other services, worried about collisions.
05:12 Priya Nambiar: we recommend reserving a /22 for Redwood in each VPC to simplify. That avoids overlap with common infra ranges.
05:20 Evan Shaw: does Redwood need public subnets?
05:23 Priya Nambiar: depends on the pattern — for PrivateLink you need interface endpoints and NAT for egress; for TGW peering you still want private subnets; public subnets aren't strictly required unless you want external egress through internet-facing NAT.
05:40 Tom Beck: audit and logs — can we pull per-request logs to our S3 or push to Splunk?
05:47 Alex Chen: yes, Private supports pushing audit logs to your S3 with encryption via your KMS, and we have Splunk/CloudWatch forwarders. We'll include the log retention and schema in the doc.
05:58 Carlos Vega: great. Also, licensing/commits: if we move forward we want a pilot in eu-west-1 then prod multi-region. Timeline's tight — compliance review by mid August.
06:09 Marta Ruiz: ok we'll aim to have the security pack and IP planning template in the next week.
06:13 Lina Ortiz: one more question, do you support static egress for function calls via third-party vendor X (they only accept a /29)?
06:21 Samir Patel: yes we can reserve small sub-blocks, but /29 per vendor may be tight at scale. We'll show tradeoffs in the IP plan doc.
06:33 Evan Shaw: what's the typical failover if eu capacity exhausted?
06:37 Priya Nambiar: you can set automatic fallback to compatible model in us-east-1 but then data residency rules might block that. Another option: pre-provision burst capacity in eu.
06:49 Alex Chen: quick recapping — we'll: 1) send IP planning template; 2) send TGW/PrivateLink design patterns; 3) include KMS, logging, SOC2 materials; 4) run latency/cost estimate for 5k qps in eu and us.
07:06 Carlos Vega: thanks, and please call out the gating items for legal and security (audit scope, KMS ownership).
07:13 Tom Beck: and also include a small checklist for network firewall rules and ALLOWED ports.
07:18 Alex Chen: will do.
07:20 Lina Ortiz: can we get Priya's contact for the follow-up workshop?
07:23 Priya Nambiar: priya@redwood.ai — i'll send a calendar invite.
07:27 Marta Ruiz: i'll coordinate the follow-up and loop in our solutions engineer.
07:30 Alex Chen: perfect. Thanks everyone.
07:33 End meeting.

Notes: brief pauses and occasional transcription errors, e.g., 'PrivateLink' sometimes transcribed as 'private link', 'KV' as 'kay vee'. Shared artifacts: Redwood VPC design template (link: https://redwood.example/doc/vpc-ip-plan), SOC2 mapping (link: https://redwood.example/sec/soc2-summary).

Action items (as recorded): Alex to send design templates; Lina to share NAT/EIP list; Priya to run latency/cost sim; Tom to share audit/KMS doc.

Questions: - Are there any regulatory blockers for routing EU data to US fallback? (customer legal team)
- Can Redwood provide per-request trace IDs in logs? (answered: yes)
